pr_title: [NativeAOT] Replace GVMLookupForSlot internal cache with generic cache similar to CastCache
pr_body:
Fixes: https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/issues/85927

- the new cache is basically a generic form of `CastCache`. It is completely lock-free and slightly faster than the currently used caching scheme.
- unlike the ad-hoc caching scheme used in GVM, the new cache is a standalone implementation and may be used in other similar scenarios.
- refactored `CastCache` can now also be used for other purposes (no longer assumes a single static instance)

The slow helper is still not tail-called, BTW. 
@jakobbotsch - do we have the same reasons here as in https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/85901#issuecomment-1538090335 or something can be tweaked to convince JIT into tail-calling in `GVMLookupForSlot`?

> @jakobbotsch - do we have the same reasons here as in [#85901 (comment)](https://github.com/dotnet/runtime/pull/85901#issuecomment-1538090335) or something can be tweaked to convince JIT into tail-calling in `GVMLookupForSlot`?

Yes, I think so.

It's hard to work around this particular limitation -- as soon as we end up with `ldloca` for a local or inlined local, we end up hitting it. You could try various patterns to avoid this, but I see many locals in the jit disasm output marked with `ld-addr-op` due to a bunch of inlining, so it's likely not easy.

> as soon as we end up with ldloca for a local or inlined local, we end up hitting it

I see. That seems hard to avoid when working with structs.

issue_context.title: [NativeAOT] consider using casting cache in GVMLookupForSlot scenario.
issue_context.body:
It looks like GVMLookupForSlot has the same properties as casting - what is cached is relatively fast, so the cache needs to be faster, on the other hand it can have certain tradeoffs like simple/lossy resizing and expiration policies, while providing faster lookups and lock-free add.

It would make sense to try using Casting cache for GVMLookupForSlot.

review_comments: Casing rotates by half of the pointer size. Should we do the same here?

Casting basically folds two pointers into a native-sized hash value and then multiplies with golden ratio and picks the topmost bits. That is to ensure that clusters of keys do not map to clusters of table indexes. The intermediate unreduced hashcode is native size and we compute it by rotating one part by half the pointer. 

Here we produce a 32bit hash (per `GetHashCode` contract). We are not yet reducing it to the desired length or dispersing among buckets - that will happen inside the cache. Our job here is only to map two pointers to as much unique 32bit number as possible. 
I think most randomness will be in the lower 16 bits, so I rotate by 16 bits. Without rotation it seems more likely to end up with same hashes for different inputs because the result will generally use fewer bits.

If I rotate by 32bit, I think the following `nint.GetHashCode()` will undo that by xor-ing upper and lower 32bit.

One other thing to note is that the use of native math in index computation inside the caches is mostly "because we can". I think using 32bit codepath for both 64bit and 32bit case would not make a lot of difference, - not for the sizes of caches that we expect here anyways, but since we can use 64bit, we use that.
Ah ok, I have missed that this goes through a regular GetHashCode.
